6.x: In the ancient Near East, “dogs” and “swine” were not metaphors for pets. Dogs were not the domestic companions we know today, but street scavengers: wild, semi-dangerous, and ceremonially unclean. Swine (pigs), were the epitome of uncleanness in the Mosaic Law. To a Jewish audience, these animals represented those who have no appreciation for, and are even hostile toward, the things of God. The holy and pearls are the precious truths of the gospel. Jesus is teaching that while the gospel is for everyone, there comes a point where sharing precious spiritual truths with someone who is mockingly hostile becomes counterproductive. It is an act of stewardship to decide where to invest your spiritual energy. There is a difference between a “seeker” who has questions and a “scoffer” who only wants to trample on your faith. Jesus is giving us permission to stop casting out “pearls” when it is clear the other person only intends to mock. Just as the disciples were told to “shake the dust off their feet” if a town rejected them (Mt 10:14), we are called to discern when our words are being wasted on those who hate the truth.

11.x: “if ye then, being evil”: even by common standard, every humans is “evil” (fallen/sinful) compared to the absolute holiness of God (Rom 3:10-12,23; Ps 51:5;58:3;Gen 6:5;Isa 64:6,etc). Yet, even in a fallen state, parental love still functions. If a flawed, sinful human father has the heart to provide for his children, the capacity of a perfect, heavenly Father to provide must be infinitely greater. “Give good things”: God does not promise to give us whatever we want, but specifically “good things.” Just as a father wouldn’t give a child a serpent (even if the child mistakenly asked for one because it looked like a fish), God often withholds “stones” or “serpents” that we incorrectly think are “bread.” The entire logic of prayer here is built on the Father-Child relationship. Prayer is not an incantation to get results; it is an appeal to a loving Parent (prayer would lose its efficacy and purpose when prayer is done towards anything that is not our Father). The reason we can “keep on asking” is that the person on the other side is not a begrudging neighbor, but a generous loving Father dying to care for & to have a relationship with His son.

12.x: This is the climax of the Sermon on the Mount, often referred to as The Golden Rule. “Therefore”: this connects this verse to the preceding passages (v7-11) about the generosity of the Heavenly Father. Jesus is arguing that since God is so gracious and gives “good things” to us, we ought to reflect that same character in how we treat others. Many ancient cultures had a “Silver Rule” which stated: “Do NOT do to others what you would NOT want them to do to you” (a command to avoid harm). Jesus turns this into a positive, active command. Passive: “I won’t steal from my neighbor because I don’t want to be stolen from.” Active (Jesus): “I will actively seek ways to bless, help, and honor my neighbor because that is how I would want to be treated.” It moves the standard from “refraining from evil” to “proactively doing good.” “the law and the prophets”: Jesus is claiming that the entire OT can be boiled down to this one principle of love and empathy. It is a parallel to the “Greatest Commandment” found later in Mt 22:37-40, where Jesus says that loving God and loving your neighbor are the two pillars upon which all the law hangs. It doesn’t require a law degree to understand. It uses our own self-interest (how we want to be treated) as a compass for how to treat others. This verse effectively ends the discussion on judgement that began in v1. If you wouldn’t want to be judged hypocritically or harshly, then you must not treat others that way.

15.x: “Beware”: in the Greek (prosechō), this is a command to “hold your mind toward” something or “be on guard.” It suggests a state of high alert or focused attention. It implies that deception is not always obvious; if false prophets were easy to spot, a warning to “beware” wouldn’t be necessary. “Sheep’s Clothing”: the sheep represents the true people of God. So “sheep’s clothing” suggests that these deceivers look, act, and speak like believers. “Ravening”: an archaic word meaning extremely hungry, greedy, or predatory. Unlike the sheep, which are communal and gentle, the wolf is a predator that enters the flock not to become a member, but to consume. Jesus is teaching that spiritual danger often comes from within the fold rather than from outside of it.

1-5.x: “Judge not, that ye be not judged”: this is one of the most frequently quoted & misunderstood passages in the Bible (other top candidates are Mt 16:18-19; Mt 28:19; Jn 20:22-23). While it begins with a famous prohibition, the verses that follow provide the specific “how-to” for making right judgements. Jesus begins by establishing a spiritual principle of “measure for measure”. If you approach others with a harsh, condemning, or legalistic spirit, you are inviting God to apply the same rigid standard to you: “with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you”. “The Mote”: a tiny speck of dust, chaff, or small splinter. “The Beam”: a massive structural timber or log used in building. They “hypocrite” is someone who is hyper-focused on a minor flaw in someone else while remaining completely oblivious to a massive, glaring sin in their own life. “Thou hypocrite, FIRST..”: this verse is key. It shows that Jesus IS NOT FORBIDDING JUDGEMENT entirely. Instead, he provides a process for correct judgment: (1) self-examination (“first cast out the beam”): before addressing someone else’s sin, you must deal with your own. This humbles the judge and ensures they aren’t acting out of pride. (2) Visual Clarity (“Then shalt thou see clearly”): Once your own sin is dealt with, your perspective is no longer clouded by hypocrisy. (3) The Final Act (“To cast out the mote”): Jesus explicitly tells the listener to proceed with helping their brother. The goal of “judging” here is not to condemn, but to assist in removal. It is a rescue mission, not a courtroom trial. If “judge not” meant “never evaluate the behavior of others”, the rest of the NT would be impossible to harmonize. For example: (1) Mt 7:6 (the very next verse): Jesus tells us not to “cast pearls before swine.” To do this, you must first JUDGE who the “swine” are. (2) Mt 7:15-16: Jesus says to “beware of false prophets” and that “ye shall know them by their fruits.” This requires a JUDGEMENT of their character and teaching .(3) Jn 7:24: Jesus explicitly commands: “Judge not according to the appearance, BUT JUDGE RIGHTEOUS JUDGEMENT.” You cannot DISCERN without JUDGING. The Greek word used for "judge" in v.1 is κρίνω (krinō). The word for "discern" or "distinguish" is διακρίνω (dia-krinō). Dia-krinō is a compound word: (1) Dia (διά): A prefix meaning "through," "thoroughly," or "between." (2) Krinō (κρίνω): To judge, decide, or separate. Therefore, “DISCERNMENT” is literally “JUDGING THROUGH” or “JUDGING BETWEEN.” You cannot perform the action of krinō (making a decision or judgment) without the process of diakrinō (discerning the difference between two things).

7-10.x: Jesus establishes a universal principle of the Kingdom: persistence is met with a response. The Greek verbs for “ask, seek, knock” are in the present imperative, which implies a continuous action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking.

13-14.x: “Strait” is archaic English that means narrow, cramped, or restricted. It refers to a passage that is difficult to pass through. “Destruction”: this refers to spiritual ruin or eternal loss. “Life”: it refers to life-eternal, abundant life in the presence of God. Jesus sets up a series of direct contrasts to illustrate the spiritual reality of humanity. The two gates: (1) The Wide Gate: it is easily accessible and requires sacrifice to enter. You can bring all your baggage, pride, and worldly inclinations through it. (2) The Strait Gate: it is small and exclusive (literally through Jesus alone). Entering it requires “agonizing” (from the Greek agonizomai) to cast off the things that won’t fit through, namely, self-will and sin. The two Ways: (1) The Broad Way: this is the path of least resistance. It is the “popular” route where one simply follows the crowd or the “spirit of the age.” It requires no discipline or discernment. (2) The Narrow Way: this is a “compressed” or “afflicted” path. It requires careful walking and constant reliance on God’s direction. It is the path of discipleship. The Two Destinies: (1) Destruction: the broad path feels easy at the beginning, but its end is ruin. (2) Life: the narrow path is difficult at the beginning, but its end is eternal joy. The majority of people choose the easier, broader path. Truth and righteousness are rarely determined by a “majority vote.” The fact that “few there be that find it” suggests that finding the way of life requires intentionality, seeking, and a willingness to be in the minority. The “strait gate” represents the SINGULAR way to God. In Jn 14:6, Jesus clarifies that he is the strait gate: “I am THE WAY, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” The gate is narrow because it is defined by the person and work of Christ alone, rather than a broad “all roads lead to heaven” philosophy.

In 2024, speaking to young people in Singapore, Pope Francis said: “All religions are paths to God… they are like different languages that express the divine.” After the Second Vatican Council of 1965, the Catholic Church did a 180 and began to express a more open and nuanced view of other religions, including the possibility of salvation for non-Christians: “Those also can attain to everlasting salvation who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel of Christ or His Church, yet sincerely seek God and, moved by grace, strive to do His will as it is known to them through the dictates of conscience.” (Lumen Gentium, 1964). This led to Catholic Bishops, like the popular Bishop Robert Barron, to teach that even a Jew, a Muslim, or anyone else can be saved without accepting Christ by simply following their conscience, since our conscience is God’s voice (he articulates this perfectly in the interview between Bishop Barron and Ben Shapiro on YouTube). The same document, Lumen Gentium 16, states that the Jews “remain most dear to God”, and that Muslims “adore the one God.. merciful and all-powerful”. Also, Nostra Aetate says that the Church “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions. They argue salvation still comes through Christ, even if a person does not explicitly know HIm. The Catechism was updated to include: “Those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but who nevertheless seek God with a sincere heart, and, moved by grace, try in their actions to do his will as they know it through the dictates of their conscience — those too may achieve eternal salvation.” (CCC 847) And: “The plan of salvation also includes those who acknowledge the Creator, in the first place amongst whom are the Muslims; these profess to hold the faith of Abraham, and together with us they adore the one, merciful God, mankind's judge on the last day” (CCC 841). This also leads people like Mother Teresa to give actual food to the needy, but refrain from sharing the actual Word of eternal life: “What God is in your mind you must accept. I cannot tell you what God is in your mind—you must accept Him. The important thing is that you are sincere. If you are a Hindu, be a good Hindu; if you are a Muslim, be a good Muslim; if you are a Catholic, be a good Catholic.” (Mother Teresa). All this, of course, completely contradicts what the Bible teaches:“Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist… Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father.” (1 Jn 2:22–23 KJV); “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” (Jn 14:6 KJV); “He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life.” (1 Jn 5:11–12 KJV); “By which also ye are saved… how that Christ died for our sins… and that he rose again the third day.” (1 Cor 15:1–4 KJV); “The preaching of the cross… unto us which are saved it is the power of God.” (1 Cor 1:18 KJV); “Without shedding of blood is no remission.” (Hebrews 9:22 KJV); “For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth(go on rejecting truth), there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins.” (Heb 10:26 KJV); “If thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved” (Rom 10:9 KJV). Meanwhile, the Quran teaches the exact opposite: “They said, ‘We killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.’ But they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him—it was made to appear so to them…rather, Allah raised him up to Himself.” (Qur’an 4:157-158); “The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; many were the messengers that passed away before him…” (Qur’an 5:75); “Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam…” (Qur’an 3:59); Allah will say: “O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, ‘Take me and my mother as gods besides Allah?’” (Qur’an 5:116); “It is not befitting for Allah to take a son…” (Qur’an 19:35); “He is Allah, One… He neither begets nor is born…” (Qur’an 11). So either Catholicism is right and the Bible is wrong, or the Bible is right and Catholicism and Islam is false and lead to perdition.

16-18.x: Jesus provides a practical “test” for the discernment he commanded in the previous verse. If false prophets are wolves disguised as sheep, this passage explains how to look past the costume to the true nature of the person. The Fruits: refers to a person’s character, their actions, and the ultimate result of their teaching (this includes their doctrine). Grapes and Figs: these were the staples of Jewish diet. Thorns and Thistles: these were the result of the curse (Gen 3) and were useless for food. Jesus is arguing that while a wolf can change its clothing, a thornbush cannot change its DNA. Eventually, the nature of the “tree” will manifest in the “fruit” it produces. To “know them by their fruits,” a believer must look for specific indicators of the “good tree.” Based on the broader context of the NT, these fruits generally fall into three categories: (1) Doctrine (The Truth Test): does their teaching align with the “Narrow Way” of Jesus or does it lead to the “Broad Way”? (2) Character (The Virtue Test): Does their life exhibit the “fruit of the Spirit” (Gal 5:22-23- love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance?) (3) Influence (The Impact Test): What happens to the people who follow them? Do they become like Christ, or do they become more prideful, worldly, or divided?

19-20.x: This verse echoes the preaching of John the Baptist (Mt 3:10). It is a common misunderstanding to read these verses and conclude that “good fruit” is the “price of salvation.” However, when examined in context and through Greek grammar, these verses actually support the doctrine of salvation by grace while emphasizing the evidence of a transformed life. First, the fruit is the result, not a requirement. In the natural world, a tree does not produce apples in order to become an apple tree. It produces apples BECAUSE it is an apple tree. The Root (faith) is the source of life. The Fruit (works) is the visible evidence of that life. If you tie a bunch of store-bought apples to a dead branch, it doesn’t make the branch alive. Similarly, doing “good works” without a root of faith in Christ does not make a person “saved.” Jesus is saying that a tree that is genuinely “good” (redeemed) will naturally, by its new nature, produce fruit. Verse 18 says: “A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit”: if salvation were by works, then a “corrupt tree” could theoretically work hard enough to produce “good fruit” and thereby become “good.” But Jesus says that is impossible. The nature must be changed first. Only God can take a “corrupt tree” and make it “good” through regeneration. Once the nature is changed, the fruit follows. Notice that verse 20 says: “by their fruits ye shall KNOW them,” not “by their fruits they are SAVED”. The “fruit” is provided for the benefit of the observer (the believer exercising discernment). It is a diagnostic tool, not a merit badge. We use fruit to identify the type of tree we are dealing with. God, however, sees the heart (the root) directly. The warning that the fruitless tree is “hewn down and cast into the fire” is a warning against false profession. This would be a “false prophet” (v 15) claiming to be a sheep but is a wolf, or claiming to be a “good tree” but produces “thorns.” The judgement falls on the tree because its lack of fruit proves it was never a “good tree” to begin with. It was always a “corrupt tree”, regardless of what “sheep’s clothing” it was wearing. “We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone.” (Eph 2:8-10; Rom 3:28; 4:3-5; 5:1; Jn 3:16; Gal 2:16; etc)

21-23.x: This verse serves as the final warning against “profession without possession”: the idea that one can claim to follow Jesus without actually belonging to him. “Lord, Lord”: the repetition signifies a claim of intimacy and zeal. These individuals are not atheists; they are people who publicly acknowledge Jesus’ authority. However, Jesus reveals that a correct “vocabulary” is not the same as a regenerated heart. Verse 22 describes people who have performed “many wonderful works”, including: (1) Prophesying: speaking in God’s name; (2) Exorcism: casting out demons; (3) Miracles: doing powerful deeds. These people are pointing to their credentials (what they did) rather than to Christ’s grace (who He is). Just because someone speaks in tongues, performs miracles, does great works in the eyes of humans, does not mean that they are saved. There is a massive difference between the GIFTS of the Spirit and the FRUITS of the Spirit. Only a regenerated heart will have the FRUITS of the Spirit, while someone whom God chooses to bestow upon a spiritual GIFT may not be regenerated. “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance…” (Gal 5:22:23 KJV). The FRUITS are inner character traits that show the believer has been reborn in the Spirit. These are expected of EVERY believer. The GIFTS of the Spirit: “there are diversities of gifts.. To one is given.. Wisdom.. Knowledge.. Faith.. Healing.. Miracles… prophecy.. Tongues..” (1 Cor 12:4-11 KJV). They are Spiritual abilities or empowerments given by the Holy Spirit for service. These are distributed differently, not everyone has the same gift. But you can have GIFTS without spiritual maturity: You can speak in tongues or prophesy.. but without love, IT MEANS NOTHING (1 Cor 13:1-2). The fruits, such as love, is what shows the true transformation. The Bible shows that a person can have spiritual GIFTS and still be sinful or spiritually immature. The clearest example is the Corinthians. The church in 1 Corinthians had many spiritual gifts: speaking in tongues, prophecy, knowledge. But at the same time, Paul rebukes them for: division (1 Cor 1:10-13), jealousy and strife (1 Cor 3:3), sexual immorality (1 Cor 5:1). Yet he still says: “So that ye come behind in no gift…” (1 Cor 1:7). They had real gifts, but were clearly sinful and immature. GIFTS don’t equal spiritual rebirth. In v. 22-23, people are prophesying, doing miracles, and still not truly belong to Christ. Why? Because they were doers of iniquity: “ye that work iniquity(or lawlessness)” (v 23). A person can operate in a GIFT but resist true obedience or holiness. God can use someone imperfect, but judgement is based on faith demonstrated in obedience, not just GIFTS. These people are not saved because they never submitted to the Father’s Will (v 21), their “good works” were actually acts of self-will and pride. “But he that doeth the will of my Father”: since Jesus says only those who do the “will of the Father” enter heaven, we must ask what that Will is. “And this is the WILL of Him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and BELIEVETH ON HIM, may have everlasting life” (Jn 6:40 KJV). Therefore, “doing the Will of the Father” is not about a checklist of good deeds; IT IS THE ACT OF SURRENDERING TO AND BELIEVING IN JESUS CHRIST AS LORD AND SAVIOR. On Judgement Day, the question will not be “what did you do for Jesus?”, but rather “do you have a personal relationship with Jesus? Does he know you?” You cannot have a personal relationship with someone you constantly offend with sin.

24-27.x: Jesus reaches the grand finale of the Sermon on the Mount. Having warned about the narrow way, false prophets, and false professors, He concludes with a parable that forces every listener to decide where they will build their life. The core meaning here is hearing vs doing. The distinction between the two men is not their environment or their ability to build; it is their RESPONSE TO THE WORD. Both men hear the same “sayings.” Both men build a house ( a life, a family, a career). Both men face the exact same storm (the trials of life and the final judgement). The difference is that one man is a DOER: he puts the teaching of Jesus into practice. The other is a HEARER ONLY: he understands the information but refuses to submit his life to it. In v 24, the word for “rock” in the Greek is “petra.” This is a crucial distinction in the NT. Petros (πέτρος): Refers to a small stone, a pebble, or a detached boulder. This is the name Jesus gave to Peter. We can see examples of this in the LXX: “..they threw stones(petros in plural form) and struck down the leader and his men” (2 Macc 1:16 LXX). Petra (πέτρα): Refers to a massive, living bedrock—a solid, unmovable shelf of stone. Jesus is saying the wise man doesn’t just build on any rock, but that he anchors his life onto THE foundational rock (petra), the bedrock of Christ’s authority. The NT consistently uses petra to identify the divine foundation of the Church and the believer’s life: (1) The Foundation of the Church (Mt 16:18): “And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter (petros), and upon this rock (petra) I will build my church..”. While Peter is a “rock/stone”, the “bedrock” (petra) is either Peter’s confession that Jesus is the Christ (Mt 16:16), or Jesus himself. Paul says: “that Rock (petra) was Christ” (1 Cor 10:4). He also says Jesus is the “Rock(petra) of offence: and whosoever believeth on him(Jesus) shall not be ashamed” (Rom 9:33). Peter also calls Jesus “a Rock(petra) of offence” (1 Peter 2:8). In fact, the consensus of the “Church Fathers” also points to this reality. There have been many studies, but an often cited one comes from Jean de Launoy (a 17th-century French CATHOLIC theologian). He surveyed patristic commentaries and arrived at these numbers: 44 fathers said the rock is Peter’s confession of faith; 16 said the rock is Christ himself; 8 said the rock is all the apostles; and 17 said that the rock is Peter personally. However, the ones that said that Peter personally is the rock (petra), like Origen, also said that we can all become rocks (petra) when we confess the same faith as Peter: “If we also say, ‘Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God,’ then we also become Peter.. For every one who is a disciple of Christ is a rock(petra)” (Commentary on Matthew by Origen). NOT A SINGLE “Church Father” interpreted Mt 16:18 as the Roman Catholic Church does today (see notes on Mt 16:18 for more detail). “And the rain descended, and the floods came”: Jesus warns the storm is inevitable. The rain is the trials that come from above (external pressures). The floods are trials that rise from below (societal), and the winds are trials that beat against the walls (emotional or spiritual attacks). If the foundation is the petra (the saying of Jesus), the house remains. If the foundation is “sand” (human philosophy, self-will, or mere religious talk), the house will not just crack, but Jesus says: ‘great was the fall.”

The Catholic Interpretation of this verse is that: (1) The Wise Man is Jesus Christ (the master builder); (2) The House is the Church; (3) The Rock(petra) is Peter (petros), on whom Christ built His Church. You can find this teaching in their popular apologetics programs like “Catholic Answers”: “Peter’s Role as the Leader of the Church” by Catholic Karlo Broussard (1/11/2024).

28-29.x: “the people”: Jesus’ sermon expanded to more than just his disciples. Matthew records the visceral reaction of the crowd, highlighting the massive shift in spiritual authority that had just occurred. “Astonished”: the Greek word is ἐκπλήσσω (ekplēssō), which literally means “to be struck out of one’s senses” or “to be overwhelmed.” It wasn’t just that the people liked the sermon, but that they were intellectually and spiritually “knocked over” by what they had heard. “His doctrine”: doctrine simply means his teachings. The crowds were not just amazed by how he spoke(his oratory skills), but by what he said (the content). He had just brought the Law to clarity and had claimed the authority to judge the world. “As one having authority”: Jesus didn’t speak as a commentator; He spoke as the Author. Throughout the sermon, he used the phrase: “BUT I SAY UNTO YOU..”, effectively placing his own words on the same level as the Commandments given at Sinai. The religious leaders of the day relied entirely on “footnotes.” They would say: “Rabbi Hillel says this..” or “As it was written by Rabbi Shammai…”. Their authority was borrowed from the tradition of men. Jesus did not cite other rabbis. He didn’t ask for permission to interpret the Law. He spoke with the direct authority of the God who wrote the Law. He didn’t just explain the Word; He was the Word made flesh.
